bib.title: Modularity for ML: Writing testable and legible code (ch. 9 of Machine Learning Engineering in Action)

question: Why do monolithic ML scripts hurt maintenance and how do modular, unit-testable designs fix it?
contributions: Contrasts a wall-of-text script (listing 9.1) with an equivalent class-based module (listing 9.3) on a distribution-fitting task
Shows a unit test for a private method and an intentional failure (listings 9.4, 9.5)

results.claim: Refactoring the script into a class changes no runtime or output; it only changes how easily humans can debug and test it.
results.setup: Listing 9.1 script vs listing 9.3 class, distribution fitting on SF Airbnb price column
results.quote: This code is functionally identical to that of the script. It produces the same results in the same amount of runtime

results.claim: Wrapping code in functions does not reduce complexity (same logic runs in same order) but reduces how complicated it is to read, debug and test.
results.quote: the refactoring doesn’t do much for the code complexity

results.claim: On the Airbnb price series the script printed a Shapiro-Wilk statistic of 0.33195996284484863 with p-value 0.0, so normality is rejected.

results.claim: Where to split the code was decided by 'how can I test this block' rather than 'what looks nice'.
results.quote: “How can I test this block of code?” than by, “What looks nice?”

results.claim: Author says monolithic ML code is common across the hundreds of companies he saw as a consultant, and such teams either hire consultants to refactor or abandon the project.
results.quote: hundreds of companies’ ML teams develop solutions, is that writing code in monolithic blocks is remarkably common

limits: No measured benefit of modularity: no bug-rate, time-to-debug or runtime data; all claims are experience-based.
Pure TDD is conceded to be very hard for non-deterministic ML algorithms; the only test shown is a deterministic ppf check.
Listing code uses deprecated APIs (normed=True, seaborn style, stat._continuous_distns, scipy version string slicing) and the author advises not running it as it is slow.
Statistics and plotting would be separate modules in a real code base; the single class is for print legibility.
practices: Prototype in notebooks but never ship the prototype to production; rewrite as modular code in MVP (p249).
Split code into single-purpose public and private methods, decided by testability (p257-258, p264).
Use descriptive names, no single-letter or abbreviated variables; code should read like text (p252, p263).
Pull hardcoded tunables into constructor defaults overridable via kwargs (p259).
Return dictionaries rather than positional tuples ('currying' in author's usage) (p259, p261).
Use static methods over global functions to avoid mutable global state (p259).
Write unit tests per private/public method with known mock data and informative assertion messages; run before merging to main (p266-267).
Do not use MLflow for one-off throwaway checks; print is acceptable there (p253).
Keep evaluation plots out of tacked-on end-of-script positions (p255).
